Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\) and \(d\in\{0,1\}\). Cohort overlap gives \(P(D=d)>0\), so every conditional probability below exists. For \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), the component factors named in \(\texttt{def:observed-slices}\) have dimensions
\[
B_x^{d,\mathcal A}\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times J},\quad
D_{xy}\in\mathbb R_+^{J\times J},\quad
C_y^d\in\mathbb R_+^{J\times(m+1)},
\]
and stochasticity gives \(C_y^d\mathbf 1_{m+1}=\mathbf 1_J\). Consistency and no anticipation identify the observed path through date \(2\) with either potential path. The conditional first-order Markov property and the common date-\(2\) kernel then give, entry by entry,
\[
 A_{xy}^d[u,v]
 =\sum_{j=1}^J B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,y]C_y^d[j,v],
 \qquad
 A_{xy}^d=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}D_{xy}C_y^d.                 \tag{1}
\]
Selecting rows \(\mathcal U\) and columns \(\mathcal V\) yields
\[
 M_{xy}^d=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}D_{xy}C_y^{d,\mathcal V}.    \tag{2}
\]

Each factor in (2) is square of order \(J\). The anchor-star condition says that \(M_{x_0y}^d\) is nonsingular for every \(y\), so the determinant identity in (2) implies that \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\), every \(D_{x_0y}\), and every \(C_y^{d,\mathcal V}\) are nonsingular. Likewise, nonsingularity of every \(M_{xy_0}^d\) implies that every \(B_x^{d,\mathcal U}\) and every \(D_{xy_0}\) are nonsingular. Hence
\[
 Q_j[x_0,y]>0,\qquad Q_j[x,y_0]>0                         \tag{3}
\]
for all \(j,x,y\), since these are nonnegative transition probabilities. Notice that no inverse of \(M_{x_1y_1}^d\) is needed.

Substitute (2) into the four-anchor product. The inverses used below exist by the two anchor-star arms, and cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
K^d
&=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_0y_0}C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V}
 (B_{x_1}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_1y_0}C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}\\
&\quad\cdot B_{x_1}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_1y_1}C_{y_1}^{d,\mathcal V}
 (B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_0y_1}C_{y_1}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}\\
&=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\operatorname{diag}_{j}
 \left\{\frac{Q_j[x_0,y_0]Q_j[x_1,y_1]}
 {Q_j[x_1,y_0]Q_j[x_0,y_1]}\right\}(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}.       \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the displayed ratios are the real eigenvalues \(\rho_j^d\). The simple-spectrum assumption makes them distinct. For the diagonal coordinate matrix \(E_j\), polynomial functional calculus applied to (4) gives
\[
 P_j^d=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{K^d-\rho_k^dI_J}{\rho_j^d-\rho_k^d}
 =B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}E_j(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}. \tag{5}
\]

Absorption implies \(X_0=e\Rightarrow X_1=e\). Hence, on \(X_1=x_0\), the predecessor is in \(\mathcal A\), and after selecting \(\mathcal U\),
\[
 m_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\mathbf 1_J.
\]
Combining this equality with (5) fixes both eigenvector scale and sign:
\[
 P_j^dm_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}[:,j]. \tag{6}
\]
Therefore the first matrix produced by \(\texttt{def:recovery-map}\) is the true \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\).

Using (1), (3), and (6), for every \(y\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 F_y^d=D_{x_0y}C_y^d,\qquad
 q_{x_0y}^d=F_y^d\mathbf 1_{m+1}=D_{x_0y}\mathbf 1_J,    \tag{7}
\]
so every divisor in \(\operatorname{diag}(q_{x_0y}^d)^{-1}\) is positive and
\[
 \operatorname{diag}(q_{x_0y}^d)^{-1}F_y^d=C_y^d.         \tag{8}
\]
The selected minor \(C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V}\) is nonsingular, so \(C_{y_0}^d\) has row rank \(J\),
\[
 C_{y_0}^d(C_{y_0}^d)^\top\text{ is invertible},\qquad
 C_{y_0}^d(C_{y_0}^d)^\top\{C_{y_0}^d(C_{y_0}^d)^\top\}^{-1}=I_J.       \tag{9}
\]
Equations (1), (8), and (9) imply for every \(x\),
\[
 W_x^d=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}D_{xy_0}.                         \tag{10}
\]
This matrix is nonsingular. As above \(m_x^{d,\mathcal U}=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}\mathbf 1_J\); therefore
\[
 c_x^d=(D_{xy_0})^{-1}\mathbf 1_J>0,\qquad
 W_x^d\operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}.      \tag{11}
\]
For \(J<m\), recovery of selected rows alone is insufficient. Using the \(\mathcal A\)-by-\(\mathcal V\) version of (1), (8), and (11),
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{xy_0}^{d,\mathcal A,\mathcal V}(C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}
 \operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)
&=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}D_{xy_0}\operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)\\
&=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}.                                     \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every predecessor row is recovered. For arbitrary \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), equations (1), (8), and (11) now give
\[
 q_{xy}^d=(B_x^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}A_{xy}^{d,\mathcal U,\mathcal S}
 \mathbf 1_{m+1}=D_{xy}\mathbf 1_J.                      \tag{13}
\]
Consequently \(q_{xy}^d[j]=Q_j[x,y]\), including possible zero non-anchor transitions. Row stochasticity identifies
\[
 Q_j[x,e]=1-\sum_{y\in\mathcal A}Q_j[x,y],                \tag{14}
\]
and absorption fixes the exit row. Equation (8) identifies every active row of the factual first-post matrix \(R_j^d\), and absorption again fixes its exit row.

Summing the recovered predecessor probabilities yields
\[
 s_j^d[x]=\mathbf 1_m^\top B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[:,j]
 =P(Z=j,X_1=x\mid D=d),\qquad
 \alpha_j^d=\sum_{x\in\mathcal A}s_j^d[x].               \tag{15}
\]
The nonnegative square matrix \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\) is nonsingular, so each of its columns is nonzero and has a strictly positive column sum. Therefore
\[
 \alpha_j^d\geq\mathbf 1_J^\top B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}[:,j]>0,
 \qquad
 \pi_j^d=\alpha_j^d+P(Z=j,X_1=e\mid D=d)\geq\alpha_j^d>0. \tag{16}
\]
This proves the formerly assumed type overlap from the observable rank condition.

Equations (1) and (8)--(15) recover the complete unnormalized component law on \(\{X_1\in\mathcal A\}\). Explicitly, for \(u,x,y\in\mathcal A\), \(v\in\mathcal S\), its cell mass conditional on \(D=d\) is
\[
 B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,y]R_j^d[y,v],               \tag{17}
\]
while for \(y=e\) it is \(B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,e]\mathbf 1\{v=e\}\). In particular,
\[
 P(X_2\in\cdot\mid D=d,Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A)
 =\frac{s_j^dQ_j}{\alpha_j^d}.                             \tag{18}
\]

The ratios in (4) depend only on the cohort-common \(Q_j\), so their strict descending order agrees across cohorts. Consistency gives \(R_j^0=U_j\) on active rows. No anticipation gives the same treated-cohort \(X_2\) under the two paths, and the common untreated first-post assumption gives its untreated continuation kernel \(U_j=R_j^0\). Iterated expectation with (18) therefore proves the causal, rather than definitional, identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_j
&=E[\mathbf 1\{Z=j\}\{\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0))\}\mid D=1]\\
&=s_j^1Q_j(R_j^1-R_j^0).                                  \tag{19}
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(X_1=e\), no anticipation gives \(X_1(0)=X_1(1)=e\), and absorption applied along both potential paths gives \(X_3(0)=X_3(1)=e\). Hence these units contribute zero to (19). By (16), division is legitimate and
\[
 \eta_j=\frac{\nu_j}{\alpha_j^1}.                         \tag{20}
\]
Finally, finite additivity over the known support \(Z\in\{1,\ldots,J\}\) gives
\[
 \tau=\sum_{j=1}^J\nu_j.                                 \tag{21}
\]
Equations (19)--(21) are exactly \(\Phi(p)=\theta_J\). Every operation uses only the observed law and the declared nonzero margins. The same derivation therefore holds for every \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal F(p)\), proving fiberwise recovery. Only the four matrices appearing in (4) determine the spectral basis; equations (8)--(13) use the anchor-star slices to transport that basis to all \(m\) active states. No equality across dates and no date-\(4\) kernel entered the proof.

Fix \(P\) as in the statement and \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal F(p)\). Cohort overlap and equality of every observed cell probability imply
\[
 \widetilde P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=0.          \tag{1}
\]
Since \(Z\) has the finite support \(\{1,\ldots,J\}\), nonnegativity and (1) give \(\widetilde P(Z=j,X_1=e\mid D=d)=0\) for every \(j,d\). Therefore
\[
 \widetilde\pi_j^d=\widetilde P(Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A\mid D=d)
 =\widetilde\alpha_j^d.                                  \tag{2}
\]
The active-frontier theorem identifies the right side throughout the fiber and derives its strict positivity from anchor-star nonsingularity. Hence
\[
 \widetilde\pi_j^d=\widetilde\alpha_j^d=\alpha_j^d=\pi_j^d>0. \tag{3}
\]
The active theorem recovers the complete unnormalized component law on \(\{X_1\in\mathcal A\}\). Equation (1) says this event has full probability within every positive type-cohort cell in (3), so that unnormalized law is the full component law. Dividing by the identified mass in (3) recovers its conditional version.

Let \(\Delta=\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0))\). Since conditioning on \(X_1\in\mathcal A\) removes a null event within \((D=1,Z=j)\),
\[
 \tau_j=E(\Delta\mid D=1,Z=j)
 =E(\Delta\mid D=1,Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A)
 =\eta_j=\frac{\nu_j}{\alpha_j^1}=\frac{\nu_j}{\pi_j^1}. \tag{4}
\]
The aggregate equality \(\tau=\sum_j\nu_j\) and \(\Phi(p)=\theta_J\) are already proved by the active theorem. Since the proof there uses only active selected minors and full-row-rank terminal factors, the common absorbing row may be rank deficient and has no positive off-exit entries. Neither date \(4\) nor time homogeneity is used here.

For the generic claim, put weight \(1-\varepsilon\) on the complete base law and weight \(\varepsilon\) on the all-exit path in each cohort. The marginal observed law is
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)P^\circ(X_{0:4}\in\cdot\mid D=d)
 +\varepsilon\,\delta_{(e,e,e,e,e)},                      \tag{1}
\]
independently of whether the added path has label \(h\) or \(k\). The base has no date-\(1\) absorbers. Absorption therefore also rules out \(X_0=e\) in the base, so the added subcomponent is separated from the retained component at the current state until both are at \(e\), where the continuation is deterministic. Conditional on \((D,Z)\), the mixture is consequently first-order Markov: at an active state it uses the retained kernel, and at \(e\) it uses the absorbing row. Consistency, no anticipation, common untreated kernels, and cohort overlap hold componentwise. Anchor-star determinants are multiplied by \((1-\varepsilon)^J\neq0\), and the cycle product cancels its four scalar factors. Thus both laws remain in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\).

Every active slice, \(B_x^{d,\mathcal A}\), \(s_j^d\), and \(\alpha_j^d\) is multiplied by \(1-\varepsilon\), with no dependence on the allocation label. The transition kernels, recovered \(\eta_j\), and spectral signatures are unchanged. Since the all-exit path has \(X_3(1)=X_3(0)=e\), it has zero contrast. Hence, between the two allocations,
\[
 \nu_j=(1-\varepsilon)\nu_j^\circ,\qquad
 \tau=(1-\varepsilon)\tau^\circ,\qquad
 \eta_j=\eta_j^\circ                                      \tag{2}
\]
are identical. If \(a_j\in\{0,1\}\) indicates whether label \(j\) receives the added mass, then
\[
 \pi_j^d=(1-\varepsilon)\pi_j^{\circ,d}+\varepsilon a_j,
 \qquad \tau_j=\frac{(1-\varepsilon)\nu_j^\circ}
 {(1-\varepsilon)\pi_j^{\circ,1}+\varepsilon a_j}.        \tag{3}
\]
Thus the two allocations change the shares of \(h,k\), and change their full conditional effects whenever their contributions are nonzero. This proves the generic frontier.

We now verify the exact specialization. Define the complete potential-path law, for \(d\in\{0,1\}\), \(j\in\{1,2\}\), \(s_0\in\mathcal A\), and subsequent states in \(\mathcal S\), by the mass
\[
 \frac18H_j[s_0,s_1]Q_j[s_1,s_2]Q_j[s_2,u_0]Q_j[u_0,w_0]
 V_j[s_2,u_1]V_j[u_1,w_1],                                \tag{4}
\]
with common potential coordinates through date \(2\), and set all other masses to zero. Direct row addition in the displayed matrices gives
\[
 H_j\mathbf1_3=Q_j\mathbf1_3=V_j\mathbf1_3=\mathbf1_3,
 \qquad H_j[e,:]=Q_j[e,:]=V_j[e,:]=(0,0,1).               \tag{5}
\]
Successive summation proves that (4) has total mass one. Setting \(X_t=X_t(D)\) proves consistency; the shared coordinates through date \(2\) prove no anticipation; marginalizing the other potential continuation gives the required type-conditional Markov paths. Equation (5) proves absorption. Also \(P(D=d)=1/2\), the support of \(Z\) is exactly \(\{1,2\}\), and the common untreated kernels are \(Q_j\). The active rows of \(H_j\) have zero exit probability, so there is no date-\(1\) absorption.

The predecessor factors are
\[
B_a=\begin{pmatrix}3/16&1/12\\1/16&1/6\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_b=\begin{pmatrix}1/16&1/6\\3/16&1/12\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det B_a=5/192,\quad\det B_b=-5/192.               \tag{6}
\]
For row \(j\) of \(C_y^0\) use row \(y\) of \(Q_j\), and for row \(j\) of \(C_y^1\) use row \(y\) of \(V_j\). Their active minors have determinants
\[
9/50,\ -3/100,\ 31/100,\ -1/20                           \tag{7}
\]
for \((C_a^0,C_b^0,C_a^1,C_b^1)\). Since
\[
 \det M_{xy}^d=\det(B_x)Q_1[x,y]Q_2[x,y]\det(C_y^{d,\mathcal A}), \tag{8}
\]
the four determinants in cohorts \(d=0,1\), ordered \((aa,ab,ba,bb)\), are
\[
 (9/16000,-3/32000,-9/32000,3/12800),                     \tag{9}
\]
\[
 (31/32000,-1/6400,-31/64000,1/2560).                     \tag{10}
\]
In particular the three anchor-star minors \(aa,ab,ba\) are nonzero in both cohorts. The cycle diagonal is
\[
 \operatorname{diag}\left(
 \frac{(3/5)(1/2)}{(1/5)(3/10)},
 \frac{(1/5)(3/5)}{(3/10)(2/5)}\right)=\operatorname{diag}(5,1). \tag{11}
\]
Conjugating (11) by \(B_a\) gives
\[
 K^d=\begin{pmatrix}29/5&-12/5\\8/5&1/5\end{pmatrix}.    \tag{12}
\]
Its trace and determinant are \(6\) and \(5\), so its characteristic polynomial is \((\lambda-5)(\lambda-1)\). This verifies every model condition and nonvacuity.

The row vector \((1/2,1/2,0)\) is invariant under both \(H_j\), and hence the date-\(2\) type laws are
\[
 p_{2,1}=(2/5,2/5,1/5),\qquad p_{2,2}=(1/4,1/2,1/4).      \tag{13}
\]
Multiplication by \(V_j-Q_j\) gives
\[
 p_{2,1}(V_1-Q_1)=(1/25,0,-1/25),
\quad p_{2,2}(V_2-Q_2)=(-1/40,-1/40,1/20).                \tag{14}
\]
Equal type masses give the stated aggregate, contributions, and at-risk effects.

Finally apply (1)--(3) with \(\varepsilon=1/5\), labels \(1,2\), and the values in (14). The active masses are \((4/5)(1/2)=2/5\). Allocating the added \(1/5\) gives shares \((3/5,2/5)\) and \((2/5,3/5)\). Equations (2)--(3) then give exactly the four displayed conditional effects, the two displayed contributions, and the aggregate \((3/500,-1/100,1/250)\). Thus the two laws are observationally equivalent but disagree in the asserted full targets, while every active target agrees.

Let \(q_d(p)=\sum_{s:D(s)=d}p_s\). Cohort overlap makes \(q_d(p)>0\), and every entry of \(A_{xy}^d\) and \(m_x^d\) is a linear marginal of \(p\) divided by \(q_d(p)\). The active-frontier proof shows that every inverse and division in \(\Phi\) has a nonzero denominator at a regular compatible law. A simple real eigenvalue and its spectral projector are real analytic in the entries of a real matrix on a sufficiently small neighborhood where the eigenvalue remains isolated. Because there are finitely many ordered eigenvalues and all pairwise gaps are positive, one neighborhood works for all of them. Matrix inversion is rational, and
\[
 C^\dagger=C^\top(CC^\top)^{-1}                           \tag{1}
\]
is analytic wherever \(C\) has full row rank. Hence the finite composition in \(\texttt{def:recovery-map}\) is real analytic on a relative open neighborhood in the affine hyperplane \(\mathbf1^\top p=1\).

For completeness, its Jacobian is computable without an eigenvector normalization. For a tangent direction \(h\) with \(\mathbf1^\top h=0\), dots denote directional derivatives. Cohort conditioning gives
\[
 \dot q_d=\sum_{s:D(s)=d}h_s,\qquad
 \frac{d}{d\epsilon}\left.\frac{p_s+\epsilon h_s}{q_d(p+\epsilon h)}\right|_{\epsilon=0}
 =\frac{h_s}{q_d}-\frac{p_s\dot q_d}{q_d^2}.              \tag{2}
\]
For every invertible matrix, \(\dot M^{-1}=-M^{-1}\dot M M^{-1}\); the product rule therefore differentiates \(K^d\). For the simple spectral system,
\[
 \dot\rho_j=\operatorname{tr}(P_j\dot K),
 \qquad
 \dot P_j=\sum_{k\ne j}
 \frac{P_k\dot K P_j+P_j\dot K P_k}{\rho_j-\rho_k}.      \tag{3}
\]
Differentiating the recovery displays gives
\[
 \dot B_{x_0}^{\mathcal U}[:,j]=\dot P_jm_{x_0}^{\mathcal U}+P_j\dot m_{x_0}^{\mathcal U},
 \quad
 \dot F_y=-B_{x_0}^{-1}\dot B_{x_0}F_y+B_{x_0}^{-1}\dot A_{x_0y},
 \quad \dot q_{x_0y}=\dot F_y\mathbf1_{m+1},             \tag{4}
\]
\[
 \dot C_y[j,:]=\{\dot F_y[j,:]-\dot q_{x_0y}[j]C_y[j,:]\}/q_{x_0y}[j]. \tag{5}
\]
Writing \(N=(C_{y_0}C_{y_0}^\top)^{-1}\),
\[
 \dot C_{y_0}^\dagger=\dot C_{y_0}^\top N-C_{y_0}^\top N
 (\dot C_{y_0}C_{y_0}^\top+C_{y_0}\dot C_{y_0}^\top)N,  \tag{6}
\]
and consequently
\[
 \dot W_x=\dot A_{xy_0}C_{y_0}^\dagger+A_{xy_0}\dot C_{y_0}^\dagger,
 \quad \dot c_x=W_x^{-1}(\dot m_x-\dot W_xc_x),          \tag{7}
\]
\[
 \dot B_x^{\mathcal U}=\dot W_x\operatorname{diag}(c_x)+W_x\operatorname{diag}(\dot c_x). \tag{8}
\]
The product rule applied to
\(B_x^{\mathcal A}=A_{xy_0}^{\mathcal A,\mathcal V}(C_{y_0}^{\mathcal V})^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(c_x)\)
and to (13)--(15) of the active proof yields \(\dot Q_j,\dot R_j,\dot s_j\). Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot\nu_j
&=\dot s_j^1Q_j(R_j^1-R_j^0)+s_j^1\dot Q_j(R_j^1-R_j^0)\\
&\quad+s_j^1Q_j(\dot R_j^1-\dot R_j^0),
\qquad \dot\tau=\sum_{j=1}^J\dot\nu_j.                  \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
Equations (2)--(9) determine \(J_\Phi(p)h\), including the derivatives of all active masses.

Let \(\mathcal S_0\) be the actual finite support stratum and suppose \(p_s>0\) for \(s\in\mathcal S_0\). Its saturated scores are exactly the functions \(a\) with \(E_Pa(O)=0\), because \(p_{\epsilon,s}=p_s\{1+\epsilon a(s)\}\) is a probability vector for sufficiently small \(|\epsilon|\). Along this path,
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\Phi(p_\epsilon)\right|_{0}
 =J_\Phi(p)\sum_sp_se_sa(s)
 =E_P\{J_\Phi(p)(e_O-p)a(O)\}=E_P\{G_p(O)a(O)\}.         \tag{10}
\]
Also \(E_PG_p(O)=0\). Since the saturated tangent space is all of \(L_2^0(P)\), (10) uniquely identifies \(G_p\) as the canonical gradient. Its covariance is
\[
 E_P[G_p(O)G_p(O)^\top]
 =J_\Phi(p)\{\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\}J_\Phi(p)^\top=\Sigma(p). \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, if a centered influence vector \(H\) represents the derivative of any regular asymptotically linear estimator, then (10) gives
\[
 E_P\{(H-G_p)a\}=0\qquad\text{for every }a\in L_2^0(P).
\]
Taking each coordinate of \(H-G_p\) as a score shows \(H=G_p\) almost surely. Thus (11) is the saturated information bound.
The exact empirical identity
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat p-p)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(e_{O_i}-p)   \tag{12}
\]
and Taylor expansion of the analytic map give
\[
 \sqrt n\{\Phi(\widehat p)-\Phi(p)\}
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nG_p(O_i)+o_P(1).                   \tag{13}
\]
Thus the plug-in has the canonical influence function and attains the saturated finite-multinomial bound. No efficiency claim for the smaller restricted Markov model is made.

Let \(\mathcal K_\kappa\) be the set of \(N_m\)-cell vectors induced by \(\mathcal P_\kappa\). It is compact by \(\texttt{def:buffered-class}\). The finite margin vector contains every inverse, division, pairwise eigengap, normalization, and label margin used by \(\Phi\), while the variance buffer covers every reported diagonal. Population margins are at least \(2\kappa\), whereas the empirical guard uses \(\kappa\).

Analyticity and compactness give \(r>0\) such that the relative closed \(r\)-neighborhood of \(\mathcal K_\kappa\) lies in the analytic domain and passes every algebraic and variance guard at level \(\kappa\). On this neighborhood,
\[
 L_1=\sup_q\|J_\Phi(q)\|<\infty,
 \qquad L_2=\sup_q\|D^2\Phi(q)\|<\infty.                \tag{1}
\]
Support legality holds almost surely under every class member. Direct multinomial calculation gives
\[
 E_P\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2=\frac{1-\|p\|_2^2}{n}\leq\frac1n,
\]
and hence
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}P(\|\widehat p-p\|_2>r)\leq\frac1{nr^2}. \tag{2}
\]
This proves uniform guard acceptance.

Taylor's formula on the event in (2) gives
\[
 \left\|\sqrt n\{\Phi(\widehat p)-\Phi(p)-J_\Phi(p)(\widehat p-p)\}\right\|
 \leq\frac{L_2}{2}\sqrt n\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2.          \tag{3}
\]
Markov's inequality bounds the probability that the right side exceeds \(\epsilon\) by \(L_2/(2\epsilon\sqrt n)\). Using \(\Phi(p)=\theta_J\) from the active-frontier theorem and the exact multinomial identity proves the uniform linear representation.

The empirical covariance has the exact form
\[
 \widehat\Sigma=J_\Phi(\widehat p)
 \{\operatorname{diag}(\widehat p)-\widehat p\widehat p^\top\}
 J_\Phi(\widehat p)^\top.                                \tag{4}
\]
The right side is uniformly continuous on the compact neighborhood, so (2) proves uniform covariance consistency. In particular, every reported empirical diagonal exceeds \(\kappa\) with probability tending to one uniformly. No covariance inverse is used.

It remains to prove coverage at possibly singular correlation limits. Take an arbitrary sequence \(P_n\in\mathcal P_\kappa\). A subsequence has \(p_n\to p_\star\), and continuity gives \(\Sigma(p_n)\to\Sigma(p_\star)\). For \(\ell\in\mathcal L\), put
\[
 \sigma_{n,\ell}^2=\Sigma_{\ell\ell}(p_n)\geq2\kappa,
 \qquad Y_{n,i,\ell}=G_{p_n,\ell}(O_i)/\sigma_{n,\ell}.
\]
The vectors \(Y_{n,i}\) are centered and uniformly bounded by (1) and the diagonal buffer. After a further subsequence their correlation matrices \(\Gamma_n\) converge to a positive-semidefinite unit-diagonal matrix \(\Gamma_\star\), which may be singular. For fixed \(u\), a third-order expansion with a uniform bounded remainder gives
\[
 E_{P_n}e^{iu^\top Y_{n,1}/\sqrt n}
 =1-\frac{u^\top\Gamma_nu}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}).              \tag{5}
\]

prose_updates.tldr: For a finite active state space of size \(m\) and a known type count \(2\leq J\leq m\), four anchor slices determine the spectral basis and \(2m-1\) observable anchor-star selected minors transport it to every active state. Projectors, stochastic row sums, a full-row-rank pseudoinverse, and a full-predecessor-row transport formula recover active component sublaws, type contributions, at-risk effects, and the aggregate first-post ATT despite a common absorbing state and possible initial absorption. Anchor-star nonsingularity itself implies positive active and full type masses. The no-date-\(1\)-absorption subface additionally identifies full type shares and conditional type effects. The resulting \(N_m=2\sum_{r=0}^5m^r\)-cell map has an explicit saturated multinomial canonical gradient and guarded uniform Gaussian-multiplier bands under singular correlation; no restricted-model efficiency claim is made.

The generalized result distinguishes the full type share \(\pi_j^d\), the active share \(\alpha_j^d\), the unnormalized contribution \(
u_j\), and the at-risk effect \(\eta_j\). Anchor-star slices identify \(\alpha_j^d\), \(
u_j\), and \(\eta_j=
u_j/\alpha_j^1\), with positivity derived from nonsingularity. They cannot allocate already-absorbed zero-effect mass across latent labels, so full shares and full conditional effects need not be identified. If date-\(1\) absorption is absent, \(\pi_j^d=\alpha_j^d\) and \(	au_j=\eta_j\). The paper does not parameterize the smaller restricted Markov observed-law image, compute its score Jacobian, or claim its efficiency bound or an attaining estimator. The exact multiplier quantile is the mathematical object; a fixed Monte Carlo draw count needs separate approximation analysis. Weak eigengaps, changing selected-minor rank, unknown \(J\), clustered sampling, and approximate common kernels remain outside the result.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The paper proves a sufficient constructive frontier for fixed finite \(m\), known \(2\leq J\leq m\), fixed ex ante selected sets and anchor pairs, observable anchor-star nonsingularity, distinct common cycle signatures, cohort overlap, type-conditional first-order Markov potential paths, no anticipation, absorption, and common untreated date-\(2\) and first-post kernels. It derives rather than assumes type positivity. It does not establish necessity beyond the explicit initial-absorber allocation family, identify unknown type count, handle weak or complex off-model spectra, justify dependent-panel inference, or exploit date \(4\) restrictions for efficiency. Full conditional type effects require no date-\(1\) absorption; the broad class identifies active sublaws, contributions, at-risk effects, and the aggregate.
